paragraphs: The paper studies how to group network nodes according to their structural roles. Such groups can help summarize connectivity, support smaller models of processes running on a network, and provide useful inputs to graph analysis. The authors examine how this goal differs from community detection, making the meaning of a node’s role a central part of the problem.

Their contribution combines a definition of node roles with two optimization objectives for extracting them. These objectives draw on equitable partitions, graph-isomorphism tests, and the Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm. This gives role discovery a mathematical target: an algorithm can search for partitions that satisfy the proposed structural criteria approximately, rather than relying only on an informal idea of similar roles.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees and evaluate the approach using a new role-infused partition benchmark. This benchmark generates networks whose nodes receive different roles probabilistically. It supplies a controlled setting for testing role extraction, connecting the proposed definition and optimization objectives to networks with deliberately constructed role structure.
neurips-2023-an-optimization-based-appro.tldr: The paper defines structural node roles through graph partitioning objectives and evaluates their recovery on a new probabilistic network benchmark.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a neural network’s training process can help explain its performance on unseen data. It studies networks trained with gradient flow, including its stochastic form, and connects their changing losses to the theory of kernel machines. This makes the route taken during learning part of the analysis of generalization.

The central construction is the loss path kernel. It measures how similarly two examples’ loss gradients behave along the training path. Instead of describing similarity using only a fixed representation, the kernel incorporates agreement across the learning process. The authors use this connection to derive a generalization upper bound that applies to general neural network architectures.

The paper reports that the bound is tight and strongly correlated with actual generalization error. It also uses the analysis to guide neural architecture search, where candidate network designs must be assessed. Numerical experiments show favorable performance against state-of-the-art search algorithms, giving the theoretical connection a practical application in choosing network architectures.
neurips-2023-analyzing-generalization-of.tldr: A kernel built from loss-gradient agreement along training yields a generalization bound and helps guide neural architecture search.

paragraphs: AUDIT addresses audio editing through instructions that describe a requested change. Earlier diffusion approaches condition editing on a description of the complete desired recording, even when a user only needs a local modification. The paper also identifies unwanted changes to unaffected audio and a lack of editing-specific training as problems with those approaches.

The authors construct training examples containing an instruction, an input recording, and its edited output. A latent diffusion model learns to generate the output while conditioned on both the instruction and the original audio. Comparing input and output recordings lets it learn which segments require modification, supporting edits that preserve portions outside the requested change.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on objective and subjective measures across several editing tasks, including adding, removing, and replacing sounds, inpainting, and super-resolution. These findings support training directly for editing rather than relying solely on output descriptions. The practical benefit is an interface centered on what should change, with the existing recording providing the remaining context.
neurips-2023-audit-audio-editing-by-foll.tldr: AUDIT trains a latent diffusion model on audio-editing examples so users can request changes without describing the entire desired recording.

paragraphs: Back-Modality proposes a general way to create additional training examples by moving data between modalities. An example begins in one form, passes through an intermediate form, and is then converted back. This round trip supplies a framework for producing variations of data through transformations across different forms of representation.

The framework has two uses. The transformation cycle itself acts as data augmentation, and the intermediate modality provides a place to apply other augmentation methods. For example, an image can benefit from augmentation techniques designed for text when text serves as the intermediate representation. This allows techniques developed for one modality to contribute to learning in another.

The authors demonstrate three versions, called back-captioning, back-imagination, and back-speech. They evaluate the framework on image classification, sentiment classification, and textual entailment, reporting consistent performance improvements when training data is scarce. The findings support cross-modal transformation as a useful augmentation strategy in those settings, with the intermediate representation becoming an active part of how new training examples are generated.
neurips-2023-back-modality-leveraging-mo.tldr: Back-Modality augments data by converting it into another modality and back, improving evaluated tasks when training data is scarce.

paragraphs: BasisFormer forecasts time series using learned bases: patterns that help represent observations and provide references for future behavior. The paper argues that useful bases must both fit the dataset and have distinct relationships with individual series. Its architecture learns these patterns and how to combine them within one forecasting system.

The method first learns bases through a self-supervised contrastive procedure that treats historical and future sections as two views. A Coef module then uses bidirectional cross-attention to measure similarity between a series and the historical parts of the bases. A Forecast module uses those coefficients to select and combine the future parts, turning relationships found in the observed history into predictions.

Experiments on six datasets report improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods of 11.04% for univariate forecasting and 15.78% for multivariate forecasting. The approach matters because its learned bases connect historical matching with future construction. That structure also provides an interpretable organization for the forecast: predictions are assembled from bases according to their measured relevance.
neurips-2023-basisformer-attention-based.tldr: BasisFormer learns interpretable time-series bases and uses attention-derived similarities to combine their future patterns into forecasts.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the difficulty of creating paired images and captions with small counterfactual changes. Such examples are useful for examining whether models depend on misleading correlations, but producing corresponding changes across both image and text is challenging. The authors aim to make this kind of multimodal data easier to generate at scale.

Their framework uses text-to-image diffusion models to automate counterfactual generation. They apply it to MS-COCO to create COCO-Counterfactuals, a dataset of paired images and captions. Human evaluations assess the quality of the generated examples, providing evidence about the resulting data in addition to measurements of model performance.

The experiments show that existing multimodal models find these counterfactual pairs challenging. The authors also use the dataset to augment training and demonstrate improved generalization outside the training domain. These two findings give the dataset complementary roles: it can reveal weaknesses in image-text understanding and supply additional training examples that help address generalization. The framework and dataset are publicly available.
neurips-2023-coco-counterfactuals-automa.tldr: COCO-Counterfactuals uses diffusion-generated image-text variations to challenge multimodal models and improve their out-of-domain generalization through augmentation.

paragraphs: CoDet studies how to connect words in captions with the image regions they describe. This alignment is important for learning object representations in open-vocabulary detection. Existing approaches rely on vision-language models to establish the connection, which can introduce problems with localization accuracy or generalization.

The proposed approach turns alignment into a search for objects that recur across related images. It groups images whose captions mention a shared concept, then uses visual similarities to identify recurring objects within the group. Those objects are aligned with the shared concept. The key intuition is that repeated mentions across images can provide evidence about which visual regions correspond to a word, without requiring a previously aligned vision-language space.

Experiments report strong detection performance and benefits from scaling the visual backbone. On OV-LVIS, the scaled model reaches 37.0 APᵐ for novel categories and 44.7 APᵐ overall, exceeding the previous state of the art by 4.2 and 9.8 respectively. These results support co-occurrence as a useful source of region-word supervision.
neurips-2023-codet-co-occurrence-guided-.tldr: CoDet aligns caption concepts with image regions by finding visually recurring objects across images that mention the same concept.

paragraphs: The paper asks how organizations can combine information using sensitive shared attributes while preserving privacy. Its motivating example links hospital and airline data through email addresses to study a relationship between travel and illness. A direct join would enable the analysis but expose sensitive information through the linking process.

The proposed method lets one organization produce a private sketch of its dataset and another privately join its own data with that sketch. It satisfies pure differential privacy and supports approximate answers to linear queries and optimization problems over the joined data. The sketch therefore enables useful computations without requiring publication of the original dataset.

A distinguishing feature is that the process is non-interactive: the sender and receiver do not need the interaction required by approaches such as secure function evaluation. The sketch can consequently be placed in a public repository for other organizations to join with. Theoretical analysis and extensive empirical results support its accuracy, connecting privacy-preserving publication with reusable opportunities for data discovery.
neurips-2023-creating-a-public-repositor.tldr: A publicly shareable, differentially private dataset sketch enables non-interactive joins and approximate analysis over sensitive linking attributes.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making with generalized linear bandits when rewards can have heavy tails. This setting allows unusually large reward values that do not fit the bounded or sub-Gaussian assumptions used by many existing methods. The analysis assumes a bounded moment of order 1 + epsilon, where epsilon is greater than zero and at most one.

The authors propose two algorithms, one based on truncation and another on a mean-of-medians construction. Both achieve nearly optimal regret scaling as d times T to the power 1/(1 + epsilon), up to logarithmic factors. Here, d describes the contextual dimension and T the number of decision rounds. The bound characterizes how performance depends on both problem size and the reward-moment assumption.

The truncation method supports online learning, while the mean-of-medians method uses only logarithmically many rewards and one estimator per epoch. At epsilon equal to one, the methods improve existing regret bounds by a logarithmic factor. Numerical experiments support their benefits, complementing the efficiency properties and theoretical guarantees.
neurips-2023-efficient-algorithms-for-ge.tldr: Two efficient generalized linear bandit algorithms achieve nearly optimal regret under a bounded heavy-tail moment assumption.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, trains neural networks by considering how much their loss can increase when parameters are perturbed nearby. It seeks flatter regions of the loss landscape, an approach associated with better generalization. The paper examines a weakness in the adversary that supplies these parameter perturbations during training.

The authors argue that an overly friendly adversary can restrict SAM’s generalization benefits. They propose variance suppression, called VaSSO, to stabilize that adversary. The approach focuses on making the perturbation mechanism more stable, addressing how SAM searches for challenging nearby parameter settings. The paper provides a proof of stability for the proposed method.

Reported experiments show numerical improvements over SAM in image classification and machine translation, illustrating benefits across different model tasks. Additional experiments find improved robustness when training labels contain high levels of noise. Together, these results connect adversary stabilization with better observed generalization and label-noise tolerance, while the stability analysis supplies theoretical support for the mechanism behind the method.
neurips-2023-enhancing-sharpness-aware-o.tldr: VaSSO stabilizes SAM’s parameter-perturbation adversary through variance suppression, improving reported performance and robustness to label noise.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether explanations respect the symmetries of the models they describe. Its setting is neural networks whose predictions stay unchanged under a specified group of transformations. If an explanation faithfully represents such a model, its behavior under those transformations should agree with the model’s invariance.

The authors formalize this requirement using explanation invariance and equivariance, drawing on geometric deep learning. Invariance concerns explanations remaining unchanged, while equivariance concerns their changing consistently with a transformation. This framework yields two metrics for measuring explanation robustness relative to the model’s symmetry group, along with theoretical guarantees for some popular interpretability methods.

The paper also develops a systematic way to increase an interpretability method’s invariance with respect to a symmetry group. Experiments apply the metrics across models associated with different modalities and symmetries, leading to five guidelines for producing robust explanations. The contribution makes symmetry agreement a concrete, testable aspect of explanation quality for the class of invariant models under consideration.
neurips-2023-evaluating-the-robustness-o.tldr: The paper turns agreement with model symmetries into measurable explanation-robustness criteria, theoretical guarantees, and a method for improving invariance.

paragraphs: The paper tackles learning detailed visual distinctions when training labels describe only broad categories. This limited supervision makes fine-grained recognition difficult, particularly when only a few examples are available for the detailed recognition task. The authors seek representations that retain useful distinctions beyond the granularity explicitly provided by the labels.

Their method places visual embeddings in hyperbolic space, which supports hierarchical relationships and offers expressive capacity useful for modeling fine-grained objects. It then introduces hierarchical cosine margins: relatively large similarity margins between coarse classes and smaller margins between fine classes. These requirements adapt separation in the representation to the level of the hierarchy.

Applying similarity margins in hyperbolic space is a substantive part of the contribution, since familiar Euclidean-space margin methods do not transfer trivially. Experiments on five benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance over competing methods. The findings support combining hierarchical geometry with different margins at different levels to improve coarse-to-fine generalization, including the challenging setting of few-shot fine-grained recognition.
neurips-2023-hyperbolic-space-with-hiera.tldr: Hyperbolic visual embeddings with hierarchical cosine margins improve fine-grained learning from coarse labels in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a backdoor can be introduced by corrupting training labels while leaving training images unchanged. Conventional backdoor attacks modify both images and labels, which encouraged the view that clean training images offered protection. The question matters when labels come from potentially malicious third parties, including crowdsourced annotation and knowledge distillation.

The authors introduce FLIP, an approach to label-only backdoor attacks built on trajectory matching, a technique previously introduced for dataset distillation. Its objective is to influence predictions on images containing an attacker-defined trigger through label corruption alone. The study therefore examines whether the labeling channel can create targeted behavior without modifying the training images.

Evaluations cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet across four architectures. In the reported CIFAR-10 result, corrupting 2% of labels produces a 99.4% attack success rate with a 1.8% drop in clean test accuracy. This demonstrates that strong backdoor behavior can coexist with largely preserved ordinary accuracy, and that unchanged training images alone do not establish protection in the studied settings.
neurips-2023-label-poisoning-is-all-you-.tldr: FLIP demonstrates that corrupting training labels alone can implant a highly successful image backdoor while largely preserving clean accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a neural network’s sequence of training updates relates to its generalization error. The setting includes gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. Instead of analyzing only the trained network, the authors study how each update contributes to the change in generalization error as learning proceeds.

That step-by-step perspective leads to a new generalization bound incorporating more information about the learning trajectory. The bound depends on the trajectory’s complexity and on the ratio between training-set bias and diversity. It therefore connects the path followed by optimization with properties of the data, making both part of the proposed explanation for generalization.

Experiments show that the method captures generalization error throughout training and tracks changes associated with different learning rates and levels of label noise. These observations support learning trajectories as useful indicators of generalization behavior. The practical significance is a view of generalization that can follow the training process itself, rather than supplying only a description of the final network.
neurips-2023-learning-trajectories-are-g.tldr: Analyzing individual training updates yields a trajectory-based generalization bound that empirically tracks error as training conditions change.

paragraphs: The paper studies statistical inference for multinomial logistic regression when the number of features and the number of samples are of comparable size. Classical large-sample results are expected to fail in this high-dimensional setting, as previously documented for binary logistic regression. The authors address classification problems with three or more classes.

Their analysis concerns the maximum-likelihood estimator, which also minimizes cross-entropy, on null covariates: features considered under a no-effect hypothesis. They establish asymptotic normality and chi-square results for this setting. These distributions supply a theoretical basis for assessing whether an observed feature estimate provides evidence of significance when dimensionality grows alongside sample size.

The resulting methodology produces feature-significance tests and associated p-values. Extensive experiments on synthetic data corroborate the asymptotic theory and the validity of the proposed p-values. The contribution is specifically about inference on null covariates in high-dimensional multiclass models, extending the statistical analysis beyond the binary case while retaining that stated scope for its guarantees.
neurips-2023-multinomial-logistic-regres.tldr: New asymptotic results enable feature-significance testing for null covariates in high-dimensional multinomial logistic regression.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many observations are needed to identify the best option with a fixed confidence level while satisfying global differential privacy. This question matters for adaptive decisions involving sensitive data. The authors first derive a lower bound that applies to any qualifying algorithm, quantifying a fundamental cost of privacy.

The lower bound suggests two regimes. With a small privacy budget, corresponding to stronger privacy, difficulty depends jointly on privacy and a new quantity called Total Variation Characteristic Time. With a large budget, the lower bound reduces to the classical non-private bound. This distinction describes how the theoretical sampling requirement changes with privacy strength.

The authors then propose AdaP-TT, a private version of the Top Two algorithm. It uses adaptive episodes specific to each arm and adds Laplace noise. Its asymptotic sample-complexity upper bound matches the lower bound up to multiplicative constants in the high-privacy regime. Experimental analysis supports the theory, linking the fundamental lower bound to an algorithm with a corresponding guarantee.
neurips-2023-on-the-complexity-of-differ.tldr: The paper characterizes privacy-dependent sampling limits for best-arm identification and proposes an algorithm matching them up to constants under strong privacy.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search, particularly DARTS, can produce networks dominated by skip connections. Because these operations have no learned parameters, excessive selection of them can lead to architectures with collapsed performance. The paper investigates why the search process develops this preference and proposes a way to make it more robust.

The authors attribute the problem to a mismatch between two parts of training. Parameterized operations can overfit the training data, while the parameters governing architecture selection are learned from validation data. Under this explanation, overfitting changes how the candidate operations appear to the architecture-selection process, encouraging undesirable dominance by skip connections.

Their response is operation-level early stopping, or OLES, which targets the proposed overfitting mechanism within the search. The method is presented as adding no computational overhead. Extensive experiments support both the authors’ hypothesis and the effectiveness of OLES. The contribution connects a specific failure mode in architecture selection to the training behavior of individual operations, providing a focused intervention within DARTS.
neurips-2023-operation-level-early-stopp.tldr: OLES uses operation-level early stopping to address overfitting that the authors link to skip-connection dominance in DARTS.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning first builds a graph of relationships between samples and then uses that graph to infer missing labels. The paper focuses on graph construction, arguing that this stage deserves attention because it shapes the label-inference problem that follows. A better inference procedure still depends on the relationships supplied by its graph.

The authors propose a theoretically motivated optimal asymmetric graph structure for label inference. Their design distinguishes the roles of labeled and unlabeled nodes instead of treating them uniformly. This distinction leads to an efficient block-wise graph-learning algorithm with a global convergence guarantee, making the graph’s structure reflect the different information available from the two node types.

The paper also explores benefits such as improved robustness to noisy node features. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superiority over state-of-the-art graph construction methods for semi-supervised learning. These findings support designing the graph around the downstream inference task, with asymmetry and separate treatment of node roles serving as central parts of the construction.
neurips-2023-optimal-block-wise-asymmetr.tldr: A block-wise asymmetric graph design distinguishes labeled from unlabeled nodes to improve semi-supervised label inference.

paragraphs: PromptIR addresses image restoration when the corruption type and severity are not known in advance. Many restoration methods generalize poorly across different degradations, creating a need for separate models and a way to choose among them. The paper aims to restore varied degraded images within an all-in-one approach.

Its method uses a small set of lightweight prompts to encode information specific to the degradation. These prompts dynamically guide the restoration network, allowing its behavior to respond to the corruption present in the image. The prompt mechanism is presented as a generic, efficient plugin module, making this conditioning mechanism the central architectural contribution.

The authors report state-of-the-art results for denoising, deraining, and dehazing, alongside the ability to handle different degradation types and levels without prior corruption information. The practical significance is that restoration can be guided by degradation-specific information inside the model rather than requiring the user to identify the corruption first. The reported tasks demonstrate how that approach supports several distinct forms of image cleanup.
neurips-2023-promptir-prompting-for-all-.tldr: PromptIR uses lightweight degradation-aware prompts to guide one restoration approach across noise, rain, and haze without prior corruption information.

paragraphs: The paper addresses alignment when different rewards represent different objectives or human preferences. A single proxy reward can imperfectly capture intended behavior, and choosing one in advance can obscure other useful trade-offs. The authors pursue a multi-policy strategy aimed at Pareto-optimal generalization across preferences, where improvement on one objective may involve a cost on another.

Rewarded soup begins with a shared pretrained model and independently fine-tunes multiple copies, each for a different proxy reward. It then combines the resulting networks by linearly interpolating their weights. The authors empirically find that models specialized from the shared initialization remain linearly connected in weight space, supporting this way of combining reward-specific solutions.

The approach is demonstrated across text tasks, image-related tasks, and locomotion control. These evaluations support weight interpolation as a practical mechanism for navigating diverse objectives. The paper’s claim is empirical effectiveness across those tasks and progress toward Pareto-optimal alignment, with the common pretrained initialization playing a stated role in the observed connectivity.
neurips-2023-rewarded-soups-towards-pare.tldr: Rewarded soups interpolate weights of models fine-tuned on different rewards to navigate preference trade-offs from a shared pretrained starting point.

paragraphs: The paper combines three related tasks: rejecting outliers, reasoning about the true model, and estimating its parameters. Treating these tasks together is intended to let a single optimization framework account for both the structure in the data and the errors that interfere with fitting it.

The authors first express the task as sparse subspace recovery in an over-embedded data space, searching for a maximum set of independent bases. They then reformulate it as continuous optimization that seeks sparse solutions for both the bases and the errors. This dual sparsity is the organizing idea: the optimization represents model structure and erroneous entries within the same formulation.

The proposed solver uses proximal approximation within alternating optimization, together with a subgradient descent procedure. Experiments on synthetic and challenging real datasets report advantages over state-of-the-art methods for fitting both known and unknown models. Applications to multi-class multi-model fitting and loop closure detection also yield promising accuracy and efficiency, supporting the framework’s usefulness across several related estimation problems.
neurips-2023-robust-model-reasoning-and-.tldr: Dual sparsity pursuit jointly models structure and errors to unify outlier rejection, model reasoning, and parameter estimation.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether pretraining followed by fine-tuning can benefit scientific machine learning, focusing on tasks involving partial differential equations. It studies transfer across changes in model size, downstream dataset size, and physics parameters pushed outside the training distribution. It also examines adapting one model pretrained on a mixture of physics problems.

The reported findings show that, with appropriate fine-tuning, transfer learning can reach target accuracy using orders of magnitude fewer downstream examples than training from scratch. This includes different tasks that can be outside the pretraining distribution. The authors observe consistent behavior across a wide range of downstream dataset sizes, making data requirements a central part of the transfer analysis.

They also find that increasing model size brings greater performance gains through fine-tuning than through training from scratch on new downstream tasks. These results hold across a broad range of PDE learning tasks. Together, they provide evidence for developing scientific foundation models, while retaining appropriate fine-tuning as an explicit condition behind the reported transfer benefits.
neurips-2023-towards-foundation-models-f.tldr: Across PDE learning tasks, appropriately fine-tuned pretrained models can sharply reduce downstream data needs and gain more from increased model size.

paragraphs: The paper investigates a possible connection between human peripheral vision and the robustness of visual recognition. Its hypothesis is that continual exposure to lower-fidelity peripheral images contributes to robust perception. The authors test a related training intervention for neural networks, which can change their predictions in response to visually subtle adversarial perturbations.

They introduce RBlur, an image transformation based on distance from a fixation point. Areas farther from that point are blurred and have their color saturation reduced, simulating the loss of visual fidelity in peripheral vision. Neural networks are then trained using these transformed images, making this variation in image quality part of their learning experience.

Compared with networks trained on the original images, RBlur-trained networks show substantially greater robustness to both adversarial attacks and ordinary image corruptions. The paper reports up to 25% higher accuracy on perturbed data. These experiments support the proposed transformation as a robustness intervention; the human-vision explanation remains the motivating hypothesis rather than an established result about human perception.
neurips-2023-training-on-foveated-images.tldr: Training on images blurred and desaturated away from a fixation point improves reported robustness to adversarial and ordinary corruptions.

paragraphs: The paper examines why accurate trajectory prediction on a fixed dataset can fail to translate into good autonomous driving performance. Common prediction measures assess how closely a forecast matches recorded movement. Yet a predictor used for vehicle control participates in an interaction that a fixed recording cannot reproduce.

The authors call this mismatch a dynamics gap. Predictions influence the ego vehicle’s behavior, that behavior changes how nearby vehicles respond, and those responses affect subsequent predictions. Each predictor can therefore induce different dynamics. In a fixed dataset, other vehicles’ responses are already determined, so this feedback between prediction, control, and surrounding traffic is absent.

The study examines this gap alongside other contributors to the disparity between prediction and driving performance. Its findings highlight a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational efficiency in downstream driving. The authors argue for interactive evaluation tied to the driving task, so that assessment captures the consequences of using a predictor for control as well as its ability to match recorded trajectories.
neurips-2023-what-truly-matters-in-traje.tldr: Trajectory predictors need interactive driving evaluation because their control decisions alter surrounding traffic, creating dynamics absent from fixed datasets.

paragraphs: The paper asks why intermediate reasoning steps can improve answers without providing new observations. Its hypothesis concerns training data made of overlapping local groups of strongly related variables. A model may learn accurate relationships within these groups and then connect them through intermediate variables to infer relationships never observed together during training.

The authors prove a reasoning gap for an autoregressive density estimator trained on local samples from a chain-structured probabilistic model. In this setting, reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias. They then investigate more complex cases by training autoregressive language models on samples from Bayesian networks, with each sample exposing only a subset of variables.

In those experiments, intermediate steps help match conditional probabilities only when the training data is locally structured around variable dependencies. Combining local observations with reasoning is also much more data-efficient than training on all variables. The results provide a specific statistical explanation for step-by-step reasoning: useful local relationships can be chained together, with the demonstrated benefit depending on the structure of training experience.
neurips-2023-why-think-step-by-step-reas.tldr: Theory and controlled experiments show how step-by-step reasoning can combine locally learned dependencies to improve inference.
